newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Europe's cash cocoa active as weather fears remain.
newsitem.headline: Europe's cash cocoa active as weather fears remain.

text.p: Cash cocoa trade in Europe picked up earlier this week as origins sold into the market as it rose and industry took cover on positions into 1999, trade sources said on Thursday.
"It has slackened off a bit now but in the market's run-up, there was good two-way business around," one trader said.

London-traded futures have climbed to around 1,145 stg a tonne, basis September, from 1,115 a week ago. New York cocoa futures hit nine-year highs this week. The market rallied again on Thursday, with Europe's cash trade saying industry buying was forcing dealers to buy back their hedges.
"The market is feeding itself," another commented.
Traders reported Ivory Coast and Ghana were the main sellers, offering main crop beans from the 1997/1998 season through into 1999. Both were said to be already well sold.
But a continuing problem for the physical trade was the rising futures price, which has increased margin calls on hedges, making it too expensive for some to trade.

Others complained of ongoing quality and delivery problems with beans bought cheaply direct from shippers. Shippers sold heavily into Europe earlier this year, most having secured the cocoa at prices which enabled them to undercut the second-hand market and still make a tidy profit.
The inferior quality of some shipments and defaults on delivery were only now coming to light, they added.

But industry customers, mindful of potential weather problems in west Africa, were taking on an increasing amount of cover. Coverage levels have been building in the past few weeks and some traders expressed surprise chocolate manufacturers were still in the market at this week's highs.
Latest rainfall reports from Ivory Coast seemed to indicate there would be no serious problems with forthcoming main crops but traders said the spectre of the El Nino weather pattern remained.
"It's definitely well installed and the threat of abnormal weather patterns is looking more real," one trader said.
Concerns were not confined to Africa, with traders saying crop levels in South America and Asia were also at risk, although the timing of any effects was difficult to predict.
"There are stories going around about the first dryness hitting Ivory Coast in mid-July, and if that happens we will see this market sky-rocket," one trader said. --Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
